description: Equipe composta por estudantes de engenharia de computação do IFCE - campus Fortaleza
summary:
GeoEcos is an interactive web platform that identifies places on Earth whose terrain resembles Martian dune fields and lunar impact craters. We built a pipeline that extracts morphometric measurements from elevation models: crater diameter, depth-to-diameter ratio, rim height and wall slope, and dune height, wavelength and crest orientation. It compares them with references derived from NASA HiRISE (Mars) and LOLA/SLDEM2015 (Moon) data. For dunes, a Bagnold physical scaling corrects for Mars’ lower gravity and thinner atmosphere, so the comparison is physically meaningful rather than purely geometric.

On a 3D globe, users explore 24 Earth sites, many in Brazil’s Northeast, matched against 9 lunar craters and 7 Martian dune fields. Each site shows a similarity score, a metric-by-metric breakdown, its climate context from NASA POWER, a photo, and an AI-generated report. The report explains the similarities and differences and suggests how NASA could use the site.

Planetary analogs are where astronauts train, rovers are tested and instruments are calibrated before going to space. Our tool makes finding them transparent and data-driven, and it highlights overlooked candidates in the Global South.
details:
We wanted to answer a simple question: which places on Earth look most like Mars and the Moon, and why?

NASA trains astronauts, tests rovers and calibrates instruments at “analog” sites on Earth, but finding them usually depends on expert knowledge of a few famous places. We built Planetary Analog Finder to make that search open and data-driven, and to bring in places that rarely make the list, like the dunes and impact craters of Brazil’s Northeast, where our team lives.

How it works. We measure the shape of the terrain the same way on every world. For craters, that means diameter, depth, rim height and wall steepness; for dunes, it means height, spacing and crest direction. Earth data comes from elevation models. Mars and Moon references come from NASA HiRISE, LOLA and SLDEM2015. Because Mars has weaker gravity and thinner air, its dunes grow differently, so we apply Bagnold’s physical scaling before comparing them. Each Earth site gets a similarity score against every planetary reference.

What you see. A 3D globe with 24 Earth sites. Click one, and its pin opens into a photo of the place. Next to it, you see its closest Martian or lunar match, a metric-by-metric comparison and its climate from NASA POWER. An AI report then explains the similarities and the differences, and suggests how NASA could use the site. The report is held to our numbers and cites the metric behind every claim.

How we built it. Python for the data pipeline, JavaScript and Three.js for the web app, Node.js on Vercel for the AI reports, which run on Gemini, and GitHub to work together.

What we cared about. Being honest with the data: missing values never count as zero, and limitations are stated openly. We also credited every image, kept API keys off the browser, and made the app usable by keyboard and on phones.
